items.question: Mid-story, the interviewer interrupts: 'You keep saying we. What did YOU actually do?' How do you recover without throwing your teammates under the bus?
items.answer: Stay inside the story and switch to first person for the decisions: which option you evaluated, what you recommended, what you personally built or communicated, and where you made the call. You do not need to claim the whole project; pick the two or three pivotal moves that were genuinely yours and describe them with 'I'. If a teammate truly owned a piece, name it in one clause and return to your part.
items.trap: Candidates either keep hiding in 'we' (by now the interviewer is convinced they cannot identify their own contribution) or overcorrect by claiming credit for everything, which collapses under the next follow-up. The interruption is a stress test of ownership, not a request to diminish the team; the bank's guidance is to use 'I' for your decisions even when the work was collaborative.

items.question: Should you memorize your STAR story word for word so nerves don't make you ramble?
items.answer: No. Memorize the skeleton: the situation in two sentences, the task, the two or three pivotal actions, and the result with a number. Practice telling it out loud a few times so the beats are internalized but the words are not. That way an interruption or an unexpected follow-up derails nothing, because you can re-enter the story from any beat.
items.trap: A word-for-word script sounds rehearsed, and it breaks the moment the interviewer interrupts or asks a follow-up you did not rehearse, because you trained for a monologue, not a conversation. The bank is explicit: keep the story focused and conversational; do not memorize a script.

items.question: What if the conflict really was mostly the other person's fault? Doesn't the 'no blame' rule force you to lie?
items.answer: No. Describe the other person's behavior factually, what they did and the effect it had, without character judgments or guessing at their motives. 'The contract changed between sprints without notice and it broke the build twice' is factual; 'he was careless and didn't care about frontend' is blame. Then spend the Action on what you did with that reality: the conversation you initiated, the assumption you clarified, the shared rule you agreed on.
items.trap: Candidates swing to one of two failure modes: sanitizing the story into 'we just talked and everything was fine' (which demonstrates nothing about handling friction, and the bank warns against stories where everyone immediately agreed), or turning the answer into an indictment of the other person (which reads as low maturity and makes the interviewer wonder about your side). Factual behavior plus your response shows judgment; blame shows none.

items.question: The follow-up lands: 'And what was your part in creating that tension?' What do you say?
items.answer: Name a real, specific contribution of yours: an assumption you didn't check, a message that came out sharper than intended, a delay in raising the issue. One sentence, no self-flagellation, then connect it to what changed: 'I now state my assumptions up front' or 'I raise friction earlier, while it is still cheap to fix.'
items.trap: 'Honestly, nothing, it was all on their side' is the naive answer and it fails twice: it is rarely true (conflicts are usually co-produced), and it surfaces exactly the lack of self-awareness the follow-up is designed to test. The bank says a mature answer can acknowledge your own contribution to the tension; the interviewer is not asking for a confession, they are testing whether you can see your own effect on a working relationship.

items.question: There is always one person who won't move. How did you handle the one who refused even after you had aligned everyone else?
items.answer: Show the sequence: you went back to them one-on-one to understand the objection, because resistance usually carries information. You checked whether the plan could absorb their concern, and adjusted where it could. If it genuinely could not, you made the trade-off explicit and, when the stakes justified it, brought the decision to the person who did own it, with the objection stated fairly rather than framed as obstruction.
items.trap: Most candidates narrate only the happy path and skip resistance entirely, which makes the story sound curated or invented, because any real initiative meets at least one resister; the bank explicitly asks how you handled resistance. The mirror failure is naming the resister as the villain of the story. The interviewer is probing whether you can work with dissent, not whether everyone loved you.

items.question: Isn't leading without authority mostly just doing the work yourself until people follow your example?
items.answer: No. Doing the work yourself is the failure mode this question is built to detect. Leadership without authority is creating the conditions: clarifying the goal so others can act, distributing work to the people best positioned, making decisions and progress visible, and enabling contributors. Personal output can be a small part, but if the story is 'I just built it all myself', you have described heroics, not leadership.
items.trap: The heroics answer feels strong ('I got it done against the odds') but it signals a bottleneck: nothing moved unless you pushed it, and nothing will scale when you are not there. The bank is explicit: be clear about how you enabled other people instead of taking all the work yourself.

items.question: How big a failure should you pick? Is it safer to choose something small?
items.answer: Pick a consequential but bounded failure: real impact on a release, a user, or a decision, but contained enough that you can explain the full causal chain and what you did about it. The interviewer needs enough stakes to see how you behave when things go wrong, and enough closure to see the changed habit, checklist, or process afterward.
items.trap: The 'safe' small mistake (a typo, a missed meeting) backfires: it reads as dodging the question and as low self-awareness, because everyone has real failures and pretending you have none interesting is itself a signal. The opposite extreme is equally bad: an unbounded disaster narrated without containment or learning raises justified doubt about your judgment. The bank asks for consequential but bounded, not for safe.

items.question: My failure was mostly caused by unclear requirements from another team. If I 'take responsibility', aren't I lying?
items.answer: Take responsibility for your slice of the causal chain, which always exists: the assumptions you made instead of questions you asked, the signals you noticed late, the verification you skipped. 'The requirements were unclear' can be true and still not be the answer; the answer is 'the requirements were unclear, and I built for five weeks without confirming my reading of them. I now force a written scope check in week one.'
items.trap: Candidates hear 'take responsibility' as a demand to confess to things outside their control, so they either refuse (and blame circumstances, which fails the accountability test) or over-confess (and turn the answer into self-criticism, which the bank also warns against). The skill being evaluated is locating your real share of a bad outcome, neither zero percent nor one hundred.

items.question: The interviewer probes: 'So did every team walk away happy?' What is the honest answer?
items.answer: Almost certainly not, and say so. State the agreement that was reached, what each side gave up, and why that trade was good enough for the shared goal: which deadline held, which requirement moved to a later phase, which team absorbed cost and why that was tolerable. Alignment is a workable agreement that the shared goal survives, not unanimous preference.
items.trap: The tempting answer is 'yes, everyone was satisfied', because it sounds like success. It fails because experienced interviewers know cross-team work always involves trade-offs, so the claim signals either dishonesty or a candidate who does not understand what alignment is. The bank is explicit: do not claim that alignment means everyone got their preferred outcome; explain the agreement and why it was good enough.

items.question: When is escalating a cross-team deadlock the right move, and when is it a failure?
items.answer: Escalate only after you have made the disagreement cheap to resolve yourself: the decision path is established, the trade-offs are documented, each side's constraint is on the table, and the remaining gap is genuinely about authority or priorities you do not own. Then escalate with the options framed, not with the conflict dumped raw. Escalating before that outsources work that was yours; never escalating lets a deadlock quietly eat the schedule.
items.trap: The naive split is 'escalation is bad' versus 'escalation gets things done', and both fail the question. Escalating on day one with an undocumented dispute reads as unable to manage sideways; sitting on a deadlock for three weeks to avoid bothering anyone reads as unable to protect delivery. The bank asks for a decision-making path with escalation only when necessary; the judgment being tested is timing and packaging, not avoidance or reflex.

items.question: How do you prove the person actually grew without turning the story into a story about you?
items.answer: Anchor the result in observable behavior that belongs to them: they shipped the next feature alone, their PRs stopped needing the same round of comments, they ran the design review, they unblocked a third teammate. Your role appears in the actions (the pairing, the questions, the feedback, the stretch task you handed over), not in the result. Avoid unverifiable claims like 'I made them a much better developer'.
items.trap: The instinct is to prove your mentoring worked by claiming the outcome ('they couldn't have done it without me'), which quietly converts their growth story into your heroics story and usually cannot be defended under follow-up. The bank is explicit: the other person's growth, not your own heroics, must be visible, and personal claims must be supported by observable improvement.

items.question: What if the person kept making the same mistake even after your feedback?
items.answer: Treat repeated feedback as evidence that your approach does not fit the learner, not as evidence about the learner. Change the mechanism: switch from telling to pairing, from abstract advice to a concrete example, from correction to a small stretch assignment where the mistake has a safe, visible cost. If it still persists, be honest about where you ended: a partial outcome plus what you learned about adapting support is a stronger answer than pretending the transformation completed.
items.trap: The two common answers are 'I repeated the feedback more firmly' (same input, expecting different output) and 'I ended up doing that part myself' (removes ownership exactly when they needed the practice). Both fail the question's real test: the bank frames mentoring skill as choosing an appropriate approach and giving ownership back, which means adapting support to the learner, not extracting compliance with your first attempt.

items.question: The interviewer asks: 'What did you drop, and what did you say to the person whose item got dropped?'
items.answer: Name the item you deferred and the message you delivered: what moved, why (the criterion it lost on), when it would be picked up, and what risk that created. For example: 'The refactor moved to the next cycle; I told the tech lead the same day, with the reason and the date, and we agreed on a temporary workaround for the worst part.'
items.trap: Candidates hide the drop because it feels like admitting failure, and construct a story where everything shipped ('I just reorganized my week'). That answer is disqualifying for a prioritization question: the entire skill being tested is choosing under constraint, and an answer with no casualty contains no choice. The interviewer is not asking whether you dropped something; they are asking whether you can say it out loud and manage the person affected, which is exactly what the bank demands: what you explicitly deferred and how you communicated the trade-offs.

items.question: Both items are equally urgent, both stakeholders are senior, and there is time for one. How do you break the tie?
items.answer: Make the criteria explicit and external: which one blocks other people's work (dependency), which one has a hard external deadline versus an internal one, which one is cheaper to reverse or redo, which one protects users or revenue if it slips. Consult the one or two people who can supply the missing fact, then decide, state the criterion out loud to both stakeholders, and set a checkpoint to revisit if new information arrives.
items.trap: 'I'd ask my manager to decide' is the reflexive answer and it fails at senior level: the question assumes the decision is yours, and delegating it upward signals you can compare options but not own the consequence. The other failure is pretending the tie does not exist ('I'd find a way to do both'), which dodges the trade-off the question exists to force. The bank asks for criteria, consultation, and a monitored plan, not a superhuman week.

items.question: How much technical detail belongs in an end-to-end project story?
items.answer: Only the detail that explains a decision. 'We moved rendering client-side' is noise unless you follow it with why: the trade-off, the alternative rejected, the constraint that forced it. Structure the story as problem, constraints, success measure, the pivotal decisions with their reasoning, and outcomes; let the interviewer pull technical depth with follow-ups and take those as deep as they want.
items.trap: Two symmetric failures: the chronological dump (week by week, ticket by ticket) that buries the decisions and signals you cannot structure a narrative, and the full architecture tour that proves depth but never reaches outcomes or judgment. The bank is explicit: tell a coherent story, not a chronological dump, and keep implementation detail only where it explains a decision. At staff level the interviewer is evaluating decision quality and influence; detail that carries no decision is dead weight.

items.question: What did you deliberately not do? Which scope did you cut, which work did you hand off, and how did you decide?
items.answer: Be concrete about the negative space: the features you cut and the criterion you used (user impact, risk, cost), the work you delegated and to whom, and what you kept because it was irreducibly yours. Then connect it to outcomes: what the cuts bought (a date held, a risk retired) and what the delegation bought (someone else grew, you stayed on the critical path).
items.trap: Candidates read 'owned from discovery through delivery' as 'did everything', so they claim the whole project personally. That answer fails twice: it is rarely credible under follow-up (who wrote every line, who ran every meeting?), and it signals the opposite of staff-level leverage. The bank asks you to state what you owned and what you deliberately delegated; a staff engineer's value is precisely what they chose not to do so the system around them could do it.

items.question: The decision went against you, and you turned out to be right. How do you tell that story?
items.answer: Compress the vindication to one clause and spend the time on behavior: you committed to the decision as if it were yours, you monitored the risk you had flagged, and when it materialized you helped contain it instead of saying I told you so. The result you highlight is trust: the manager brought you into the next risky decision earlier.
items.trap: 'I was right' is the story candidates want to tell and it is the wrong one: it centers the argument instead of the outcome, and it makes the interviewer picture someone who keeps score. The bank is explicit: if the decision went against you, the story is how you committed to it and monitored the outcome, and the result should demonstrate judgment and trust-building, not winning an argument. Being right is worth nothing in this story if the commitment and monitoring are missing.

items.question: How do you disagree with a senior stakeholder without it becoming personal or political?
items.answer: Form the view from things both of you can inspect: facts, user impact, risks, alternatives, and input from the people affected. Present it as an evaluable recommendation, not an objection: the options, the trade-offs, and what you would need to see to change your mind. Raise it directly and early, genuinely listen to their perspective (their vantage point may contain information yours does not), and if they decide otherwise, commit visibly.
items.trap: The common failure is treating disagreement as persuasion by persistence: repeating the point, recruiting allies, or relitigating after the decision. That reads as political and makes your input more expensive to hear, which is the opposite of the goal. The second failure is softening the concern so much to avoid friction that the stakeholder never actually hears the risk. The bank asks for a direct, respectful concern that is easy to evaluate, plus real listening.

items.question: How did you know the problem was systemic and not just one team having a bad quarter?
items.answer: Before designing anything, gather perspectives across the teams: where the same symptom appears, how often, at what cost, and whether the causes rhyme. One team's pain with a local cause deserves a local fix; the same pain in multiple places with a shared cause (a missing practice, a structural handoff, a misaligned incentive) is systemic. Then size the intervention to the evidence: a pilot in the most affected team, not an org-wide mandate.
items.trap: The tempting move is to generalize from the team you know best: you saw review latency, so the org needs a review SLA. That is how org-wide process gets built on one data point, and it is the failure mode this follow-up probes for. The mirror failure is waiting for perfect cross-team data before acting, which at architect level reads as unable to act under uncertainty. The bank asks you to distinguish a local symptom from a systemic issue and design a proportionate intervention.

items.question: A team lead tells you: 'This is process overhead, we're not doing it.' You have no authority over them. What now?
items.answer: First treat the objection as data: ask what specifically costs them more than it saves, and check whether the design can absorb it (an opt-out, a lighter version, or the recognition that their context genuinely differs). If the concern is real, adapt the intervention. If it is not, do not force: keep the pilot's evidence visible, let sponsorship and peer adoption do the pulling, and protect their autonomy not to adopt while the results accumulate.
items.trap: The two reflexes both fail: mandating compliance (you usually cannot, and trying burns the influence you need) and abandoning the change at the first pushback (which means nothing durable ever ships). The interviewer is testing whether you can move an organization without commanding it: resistance handled as information, adoption built as pull. The bank is explicit: build sponsorship, pilot or iterate, handle resistance, and protect team autonomy.

mcqs.question: In the Action phase of a STAR answer about a collaborative project, how should you handle pronouns?
options: Use 'we' throughout so you come across as a team player rather than arrogant.
Use passive voice ('it was decided', 'the component was built') so credit is shared naturally.
Use 'I' for the decisions and steps you personally took, even though the work was collaborative.
Use 'we' for the story, then close with a list of the tasks that were assigned to you.
mcqs.explanation: The Action phase is where the interviewer evaluates your behavior, so the guidance is to spend most of it on the decisions you took, using 'I' even when the work was collaborative (MIT CAPD: https://capd.mit.edu/resources/the-star-method-for-behavioral-interviews/). The strongest distractor is 'we' throughout: it feels humble, but it makes your contribution invisible and practically invites the follow-up 'and what did YOU do?'. Passive voice fails for the same reason: it hides ownership instead of sharing it, and a closing task list still shows assignments, not judgment.

mcqs.question: Which conflict story gives the interviewer the most useful signal about how you handle friction?
options: A real disagreement about goals, evidence, or scope where views genuinely differed and you had to work through it.
A misunderstanding that one friendly conversation cleared up, showing you can communicate calmly.
A case where the teammate was clearly wrong and the eventual outcome proved your position right.
A conflict you preempted entirely by adjusting your own working style before anything surfaced.
mcqs.explanation: The bank is explicit: choose a real disagreement, not a story where everyone immediately agreed, because a story without friction demonstrates nothing about handling friction. The strongest distractor is the one-conversation misunderstanding: it is the most common 'safe' choice, and it fails precisely because the conflict resolves itself, so the interviewer learns nothing about your behavior under real tension. The 'proven right' story adds a blame signal, and the fully preempted conflict removes the conflict from the conflict question.

mcqs.question: In a story about leading an initiative without formal authority, which behavior best demonstrates actual leadership?
options: Taking the critical tasks on yourself so the initiative succeeds despite everyone else's competing priorities.
Clarifying the goal, creating alignment, enabling others to contribute, and handling resistance.
Convincing management to mandate the initiative so teams have to comply.
Waiting until every affected person agrees before taking any visible step.
mcqs.explanation: The bank defines this kind of leadership as ownership of an outcome: clarify the goal, create alignment, invite expertise, make decisions, communicate progress, handle resistance, and be explicit about how you enabled others rather than taking all the work yourself. The strongest distractor is doing the critical work yourself: it looks like dedication, but it describes heroics and a bottleneck, not influence, and it collapses under the follow-up 'what did the others do?'. Mandating contradicts the premise of the question (no authority) and burns trust, and waiting for unanimous agreement before any visible step shows no initiative at all.

mcqs.question: Which failure story is the strongest choice for 'Tell me about a failure or mistake'?
options: A small, harmless slip (a typo that reached production) so the answer stays safe and short.
A major failure caused mainly by another team's missed requirements, showing you can survive a tough environment.
A disguised success: a project that started badly but that you turned into your best outcome.
A consequential but bounded failure where you can honestly explain your role and what changed afterward.
mcqs.explanation: The bank asks for a consequential but bounded failure you can own honestly, because the answer is evaluated through self-awareness, accountability, learning, and changed behavior, not through pretending every project succeeded. The strongest distractor is the disguised success: it is the most coached answer and it fails because a fake failure cannot demonstrate any of those four things; the interviewer simply hears the dodge. The trivial slip reads as evasive, and the version blamed on another team's requirements fails the accountability test before the story even starts.

mcqs.question: In a cross-team alignment story, what should the Result section claim?
options: The specific agreement reached and why it was good enough for the shared goal, including what some teams gave up.
That all teams ended up fully satisfied, since that is what successful alignment means.
Only that the project shipped on time, keeping the focus on delivery rather than on positions.
That the lowest-priority teams' goals were set aside to protect the most important team's outcome.
mcqs.explanation: The bank is explicit: do not claim that alignment means everyone got their preferred outcome; explain the agreement reached and why it was good enough for the shared goal. The strongest distractor is 'all teams fully satisfied': it sounds like the best ending, but experienced interviewers know cross-team work runs on trade-offs, so the claim signals either dishonesty or a misunderstanding of what alignment is. Shipping-only omits the alignment dimension the question asked about, and openly setting aside some teams' goals without the shared-goal reasoning is alignment by fiat, not alignment.

mcqs.question: What makes a 'helped someone grow' story strong?
options: A clear inventory of the techniques and concepts you taught, showing the depth of your expertise.
Evidence that the person relied on you for the hardest work while they were still learning.
The other person's growth visible in observable outcomes, and ownership handed back instead of solving everything.
A formal mentoring program you participated in, since informal help does not really count.
mcqs.explanation: The bank centers the other person's growth, not your heroics: understand their goals and current level, choose an appropriate approach, give ownership back rather than solving everything, and show observable improvement such as independence, quality, or delivery, while avoiding unsupported personal claims. The strongest distractor is the technique inventory: it flips the subject from the learner's change to your knowledge, which is not what the question measures. Keeping the person dependent on you for the hardest work is the opposite of growth, and the bank explicitly says mentoring can be informal and does not require direct reports or a formal program.

mcqs.question: In a story about multiple urgent priorities, which detail most convincingly demonstrates judgment?
options: That you completed every urgent item by reorganizing your week and putting in extra focus.
What you explicitly deferred or dropped, and how you communicated that trade-off to the affected stakeholder.
That you ranked the items with a recognized prioritization framework you can name.
That you escalated the clash to your manager immediately to protect all the deadlines.
mcqs.explanation: The bank's core point is that a strong answer never implies everything was completed at once: it names the criteria used to compare priorities, the people consulted, what was explicitly deferred or dropped, and how the trade-offs were communicated to stakeholders. The strongest distractor is 'I got it all done': it sounds like a win, but it removes the constraint, and without a casualty there is no choice, so there is no evidence of judgment. Naming a framework without criteria and consequences stays at the surface, and immediate escalation at senior level outsources the very decision the question handed you.

mcqs.question: When telling a complex project end to end, how should you handle implementation detail?
options: Keep it only where it explains a decision or trade-off; otherwise stay at the level of problem, options, and outcomes.
Cover the architecture and stack thoroughly so the interviewer can verify your technical depth.
Narrate chronologically from kickoff to launch so nothing important gets omitted.
Skip technical content entirely, because the question is behavioral, not technical.
mcqs.explanation: The bank says to tell a coherent story, not a chronological dump, and to keep implementation detail only where it explains a decision. The strongest distractor is chronological narration: completeness feels safe, but it buries the pivotal decisions and signals you cannot structure a narrative, which at staff level is itself a competency being tested. The architecture tour proves depth but never reaches judgment or outcomes, and skipping technical content entirely overcorrects: decision quality often has technical content, and the interviewer decides how deep to go with follow-ups.

mcqs.question: Your manager overrules your recommendation, and the project later hits exactly the risk you flagged. What should the story emphasize?
options: That your recommendation was documented in writing, which proved your judgment was right.
That you quietly warned teammates to prepare, while following the decision in public.
That you kept raising the concern until the manager formally accepted the risk.
How you committed to the decision, monitored the risk, and helped react when it materialized.
mcqs.explanation: The bank is explicit: if the decision went against you, the story is how you committed to it and monitored the outcome, and the result should demonstrate judgment and trust-building, not winning an argument. The strongest distractor is the written record: 'I was right, and I can prove it' centers vindication over outcome and makes the interviewer picture someone who keeps score. Quietly warning teammates is passive undermining of the decision you committed to, and repeated relitigating is exactly the behavior this question is designed to screen out.

mcqs.question: One team complains about slow code reviews. Before proposing an org-wide review process change, what does a strong scaled-change story require?
options: Rolling out the change org-wide immediately so the struggling team gets relief fast.
Gathering perspectives across teams to distinguish a local symptom from a systemic issue, then designing a proportionate intervention.
Surveying every team and implementing whichever process change the majority prefers.
Improving only your own team's review latency, since you lack authority over other teams.
mcqs.explanation: The bank requires organizational reach with a clear before-and-after: gather perspectives, distinguish a local symptom from a systemic issue, design a proportionate intervention, build sponsorship, and pilot or iterate it. The strongest distractor is majority rule: it sounds fair and data-driven, but it skips proportionality and sponsorship; a majority-preferred process can still be overhead for teams whose context differs, and adoption built on voting rather than piloted evidence tends to generate the exact resistance the story should show you handling. Immediate org-wide rollout generalizes from one data point, and staying inside your own team has no organizational reach at all.

scenarios.prompt: A candidate is interviewing for a junior frontend role and gives this answer to 'Tell me about a project or accomplishment you are proud of.' Diagnose the specific STAR weaknesses, then rewrite the Action and Result sections so the answer demonstrates personal ownership and a quantified outcome.

code.code:
INTERVIEWER: Tell me about a project or accomplishment you are proud of.

CANDIDATE: At my last job we rebuilt the customer dashboard. It was a team of
four and we used React and TypeScript. We had sprint planning every two weeks
and we divided the tickets. We improved the design and fixed a lot of bugs.
We also set up component tests and the coverage got much better. The client
was happy at the end and the dashboard looked really nice. I learned a lot
about working in a team.

scenarios.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: (1) Ownership is invisible. Every sentence is 'we', so the interviewer cannot extract what the candidate did; the only 'I' in the answer is 'I learned a lot', and it is generic. (2) The Action is a task list, not decisions: 'we divided the tickets' and 'we set up tests' describe activity, not choices, trade-offs, or judgment. (3) The Situation is padded with process detail (team size, sprint cadence) that does not help understand the problem. (4) The Result has no numbers and no consequence: 'coverage got much better' and 'the client was happy' are unverifiable. (5) There is no connection to how the candidate works or what they would carry into the role. Rewrite of Action: 'The dashboard's load time was the top complaint, so I profiled the bundle and found the table component re-rendering on every keystroke of the search box. I proposed memoizing the row computation and virtualizing the list; the team was skeptical about virtualization, so I built a prototype on one screen and measured it before we committed. I also wrote the first component tests for the two components I touched, and that pattern spread to the rest of the team.' Rewrite of Result: 'Search interactions stopped triggering full re-renders, the main screen's interaction time dropped from about 4 seconds to under 1, and the test pattern was adopted across the codebase the following sprint. I learned that a small measured prototype settles a technical argument faster than a debate, and that is still how I approach disagreements about approach.' The rewrite keeps the Situation to one sentence, spends most of the time on decisions using 'I', quantifies the result, and closes with a specific, transferable lesson.
rubric: Identifies the all-'we' narration as the core defect: the interviewer cannot extract the candidate's individual contribution.
Distinguishes a task list from decisions: the rewrite shows choices, trade-offs, and judgment, not just activity.
Trims the Situation to the context needed and shifts the weight of the answer to the Action phase.
Quantifies the Result and replaces 'the client was happy' with evidence.
Closes with a specific, transferable lesson instead of a generic 'I learned a lot'.

scenarios.prompt: You are the candidate in a semi-senior interview. You have just told a conflict story, and the interviewer pushes with two follow-ups. Answer both as you would in the room, then name one thing you would deliberately not say.

code.code:
YOUR STORY (summary): A backend teammate kept changing the API contract
between sprints without telling the frontend side, and it broke your build
twice. You talked once, he apologized, and after that everything was fine.

INTERVIEWER: 'That resolved remarkably fast. What was your part in creating
that tension in the first place?'

INTERVIEWER: 'And if he had kept doing it after that conversation, what
would you have done next?'

scenarios.modelAnswer: First follow-up: acknowledge a real contribution of mine instead of claiming the tension was one-sided. 'Fair question. My part was that I noticed the contract changes both times but stayed quiet for a few days, because I assumed they were intentional and temporary. If I had raised it after the first broken build instead of the second, it would have cost one calm conversation instead of a tense one. That part is on me.' Then the mechanism: 'When we did talk, I didn't open with the broken builds. I asked what was driving the changes, and it turned out his own upstream was shifting under him. We agreed on a rule that worked for both sides: contract changes get a message in the shared channel before merge, not after. I also stopped treating silence as intention.' Second follow-up, the escalation path: 'If it had kept happening, the next step would not be a louder version of the same conversation. I would make the cost visible and neutral: the two broken builds and the hours lost, written down, taken to our tech leads as a process gap rather than a complaint about him. If the rule cannot hold without backup, it needs an owner with more scope than either of us.' What I would deliberately not say: any version of 'he was careless', 'he didn't care about frontend', or 'I was right to be annoyed'. Character judgments turn a process story into a blame story, and the interviewer is evaluating how I handle friction, not whether I won it.
rubric: Acknowledges a specific, real contribution to the tension (staying silent after the first break) without self-flagellation.
Describes the teammate's behavior factually, with no character judgment and no guessing at motives.
Shows a mechanism that changed the working relationship (the shared-channel rule, raising friction earlier), not just a one-off apology.
Answers the escalation follow-up with a process framing (visible cost, right owners) rather than 'I'd report him' or 'I'd just keep talking to him'.
Names what was deliberately left unsaid, showing awareness of how blame sounds from the other side of the table.

scenarios.prompt: You are the senior frontend developer on a product team. It is Monday morning and three things land at once. Walk through your first two hours: your criteria, your decision, what you defer, and the exact message you send to the person whose item moves.

code.code:
09:00 - Support escalates: the checkout button on Safari renders blank and
       a handful of users cannot pay. Revenue-affecting, live now.
09:10 - Your PM reminds you that tomorrow at 10:00 there is a demo of the
       new onboarding flow to the company's biggest client, and the flow
       has a known visual glitch on the final step that you were scheduled
       to fix today.
09:20 - The security team's channel pings you: a dependency patch is due
       by Friday, and their policy requires your team's confirmation today
       that the upgrade path is compatible, or they escalate to your
       director.

You are the only frontend developer available today. You cannot do all
three before tomorrow's demo.

scenarios.modelAnswer: First, make the criteria explicit before touching any of the three: live user and revenue impact, hard external deadline versus internal, what actually blocks other people, and the cost of being wrong or late. Then reduce uncertainty cheaply, because two of the three items have unknowns that change the ranking. The checkout bug is live revenue loss, so it is almost certainly first, but I confirm scope with support in five minutes: how many users, which Safari versions, and whether rolling back yesterday's release is possible, since a rollback might be faster than a fix. For the security confirmation, I ask what 'confirmation' actually requires: if it is a compatibility check I can do in an hour, it is cheap and it unblocks their Friday deadline today; if it is a full upgrade and regression pass, it cannot happen before the demo anyway, and I say so today rather than Friday. For the demo glitch, I ask the PM the decisive question: does the client see the final step in tomorrow's demo path, and is the glitch on the happy path or in an edge case? If it is off the demo path, it moves. If it is on it, the demo becomes a genuine competitor to the checkout bug, and the PM should make that call with both facts on the table, because the client relationship is hers to weigh. Decision and communication: I take the checkout bug first, with the rollback as a parallel safety net. I message the security team today: 'A full regression pass before Friday is not possible without dropping a live revenue fix; here is what I can confirm today (a quick compatibility check), and here is when the full pass can happen. If that does not satisfy the policy, let's take both options to the directors framed like this.' I tell the PM the same day what moved and why: 'The onboarding glitch moves behind the checkout fix; here is the risk that creates for tomorrow, here is the cheap mitigation (a click-through path that avoids the glitch, or fixing it tonight if checkout closes early), and I will confirm by end of day.' Then a checkpoint: I reassess at a fixed time, say 14:00, because new information (the checkout fix turns out to be one line, or it turns out to be deep) should be allowed to change the plan. The non-negotiable for a strong answer: there is a casualty. Something moves, the person affected hears it from me the same day, with the reason and the mitigation, not after the deadline passes.
rubric: States explicit comparison criteria (live impact, deadline hardness, blocking, cost of error) before ranking, instead of jumping straight to the loudest item.
Spends the first minutes reducing uncertainty (support scope, what the security confirmation requires, whether the demo path shows the glitch) rather than guessing.
Makes a defensible call and names what is deferred: the answer contains a casualty, not 'I found a way to do all three'.
Communicates the trade-off to each affected party the same day, with reason, risk, and mitigation, and hands the client-impact decision to the PM where it belongs.
Sets a checkpoint to revisit the plan when new information arrives, showing the plan is monitored, not set and forgotten.

scenarios.prompt: You are a staff-level engineer. Tell this story end to end as you would in the interview: how you formed the view, how you raised it, what you did after being overruled, and what you did when the risk materialized. Then say what you would repeat and what you would change.

code.code:
CONTEXT: You recommended delaying a launch by two weeks to fix a data
migration risk you considered serious. The VP of Product overruled you to
hold the launch date. You committed to the decision. Three weeks after
launch, the migration corrupted a subset of user data and your team ran the
cleanup.

INTERVIEWER: 'Walk me through it: how you formed the view, how you raised
it, what you did after being overruled, and what you did when the risk
materialized. Then tell me what you'd repeat and what you'd change.'

scenarios.modelAnswer: Forming the view: 'I didn't start with the conclusion. The migration's dry runs had produced inconsistent row counts in two of five runs, and the pattern pointed at a race in the batch ordering. I sized the blast radius with the data team: which user segments, what recovery looked like, what it would cost. That turned a feeling of unease into a recommendation someone could evaluate: delay two weeks and fix the ordering, or launch on date with a rollback plan and a monitoring tripwire on row counts.' Raising it: 'I took it to the VP directly, on one page: the evidence, the two options, the cost of each, and what I would need to see to change my mind. I asked what I was missing from their side, and the answer was real information: the launch date was tied to a contractual commitment with a partner. That didn't change my technical read, but it changed my understanding of what the trade-off actually was.' After the overrule: 'I said, in the room, that I was on board and the team would make the date work, and I meant it. Then I did the two things that were still mine to do: we built the tripwire monitoring on migration row counts, and we pre-wrote the recovery runbook, so if the risk fired we would be executing a plan instead of inventing one. I did not keep re-raising the delay; the decision had an owner and it was not me.' When it materialized: 'The tripwire caught the corruption about eleven hours earlier than user reports would have, and the runbook meant cleanup started the same night instead of after a war room. I sent the VP a factual note: what fired, what we did, current state. No I-told-you-so, because the point of the note was to keep them willing to hear my next risk early.' Repeat and change: 'I would repeat the one-page evaluable format and the tripwire-plus-runbook insurance; that is what made the bad outcome small instead of defining. What I would change: I would ask about business constraints before finalizing my recommendation. My two-week proposal was technically right and contextually naive; if I had known about the partner commitment, I would have proposed the monitoring-and-runbook path as the primary option instead of as the consolation prize, and the VP would have been choosing between two launch-date-compatible options instead of overriding me.' The story's center of gravity: commitment after the decision, monitoring that converted the risk into an early catch, and a result framed as trust (the VP bringing me into the next launch review earlier) rather than vindication.
rubric: Forms the recommendation from inspectable evidence (dry-run data, blast radius, recovery cost) and presents it as evaluable options with trade-offs, not as an objection.
Commits visibly after the overrule and does not relitigate; the residual actions (tripwire, runbook) stay inside the decided path.
Shows monitoring that produced an early catch, and containment behavior when the risk fired, instead of passively waiting to be proven right.
Frames the result as trust-building and judgment (the VP seeking input earlier), never as winning the argument.
Names a genuine self-correction (surfacing business constraints before finalizing the recommendation), not a token 'I'd communicate more'.
